passage: Annual return of the Copsewood Almshouse Charity, registered number 5502, for the year ending March 31. The charity maintains twelve almshouse cottages on Founders Row for persons of limited means over sixty who have resided in the parish for at least five years. Occupancy averaged eleven of twelve cottages, with cottage 7 vacant for seven months awaiting damp remediation, completed in February at a cost of 18,400 dollars, of which 6,000 dollars was met by the county heritage fund on account of the building's listed status. Income comprised rents charged as maintenance contributions of 96,000 dollars, investment income of 41,000 dollars from the endowment, and legacies of 25,000 dollars, including 20,000 dollars from the estate of a former resident, Mrs. Adela Ferns, restricted by her will to garden improvements. Expenditure totaled 149,000 dollars, the largest items being repairs, insurance, and the part time warden's salary. The trustees, who number seven and served without remuneration, record one connected transaction: the purchase of roofing services for 9,200 dollars from a firm of which trustee Howell Price is a director, procured by sealed quotation in which that firm was lowest of three, with Price abstaining. The waiting list stood at nine at year end.
question: How much did the damp remediation of cottage 7 cost?

passage: Notice of proposed airworthiness directive, Light Aircraft Registry, reference AD-771, applicable to Skerry Aviation model SK-2 aircraft, serial numbers 100 through 262. The Registry has received four reports of cracking in the rudder hinge bracket at the location of the upper attachment bolt, in each case discovered during annual inspection at airframe times between 900 and 1,400 hours. Metallurgical examination of two removed brackets, summarized in Appendix A, attributes the cracking to fretting at an oversized bolt hole introduced by a drilling fixture used in production between serial 100 and serial 262; aircraft outside that range used a different fixture and show no findings in 5,100 fleet inspections. The proposed directive requires: within 25 flight hours or 60 days, whichever first, a dye penetrant inspection of the bracket; replacement before further flight where any indication is found; and for all affected aircraft, replacement of the bracket with the redesigned part number SK2-441C within 300 flight hours. The Registry estimates the inspection at two labor hours and the replacement at six, with the part priced by the manufacturer at 410 dollars. Comments are invited for 30 days. Three operators have already reported voluntary compliance using the service bulletin issued in May.
question: What is the part number of the redesigned bracket?

passage: Decision and order, Public Utilities Board, docket E-2019, complaint of the Grover Mill Tenants Association against Vantage Power Retail. The Association alleged that 214 tenants of the converted mill were switched to Vantage's variable tariff without valid consent following the building's sale in January, and billed at rates averaging 40 percent above the default utility tariff for eight months. The Board finds the consents invalid: they were gathered by the building manager as a condition printed within lease renewal packets, a practice rule 6.4 forbids, consent to retail supply being required to stand alone. Vantage's defense that it relied in good faith on the manager's attestation is rejected as to remedy but accepted as to penalty; the record shows Vantage's enrollment audit sampled one consent in fifty and met the industry practice of the time. The Board orders: restitution to each affected tenant of the difference against the default tariff, calculated by the Board's staff at 96,400 dollars in aggregate, payable within 60 days; interest at the judgment rate; and a compliance filing describing revised enrollment audits. The requested civil penalty is declined. Board member Ostrowski dissents in part, and would impose a penalty of 50,000 dollars.
question: What aggregate restitution did the Board's staff calculate?

passage: Application for renewal of aquaculture lease 118, Bendersund Oyster Company, six acres of subtidal bottom in Pell Cove. The applicant reports production over the expiring five year term of 2.1 million oysters sold, with survival to market averaging 61 percent, and seeks renewal on identical boundaries with one change of method: replacement of bottom cages with floating bags over two of the six acres, the cove's southern portion, where silt accumulation over the term buried cage bases twice. The floating gear, to a maximum of 400 bags, would be marked at each corner and lit per navigation rules, and the applicant encloses letters from the harbormaster and from the Pell Cove Yacht Club; the harbormaster does not object, while the club objects to any floating gear within 200 feet of the racing line it has used, by its own account, since 1958. The applicant's response, appended, offers a setback of 150 feet, notes the racing line appears on no recorded chart, and points to the lease's seniority, the ground having been under continuous shellfish cultivation since 1971. Water quality classification of the cove remains approved, save for the customary closure after rainfalls exceeding two inches. The lease fee under the current schedule is 75 dollars per acre per year.
question: What setback from the racing line does the applicant offer?

passage: Report of the monitor appointed under consent decree in Farrow v. Ridgeline Correctional Services, sixth reporting period. The decree requires the contractor to staff the county detention annex with no fewer than 14 officers on day shift and 9 on night shift; payroll extracts show compliance on 176 of 182 days, with the six shortfall days, all night shifts in July, attributed to a resignation cluster and covered by mandatory overtime that itself is limited by the decree to 16 hours per officer per week, a limit exceeded for two officers in that month. Medical intake screening within 24 hours of admission, the decree's second requirement, was achieved for 96 percent of 1,240 admissions, against 71 percent at the decree's outset; the 47 late screenings cluster on weekends, and the monitor repeats the recommendation, so far declined on cost grounds, of a Saturday nurse shift. The third requirement, quarterly grievance audits, was met, with the notable result that grievances concerning food fell by half after the kitchen contract change in the spring. The monitor rates the contractor in substantial compliance on two of three decree provisions, the staffing provision remaining in partial compliance, and sets the next site visit for the second week of January.
question: On how many of the 182 days did staffing comply with the decree?

passage: Prospectus of the Gullwing Cooperative Bakery, community share offer. The cooperative seeks to raise between 120,000 and 180,000 dollars to purchase the premises at 4 Chandler Lane which it has rented since formation in 2017, the landlord having offered the freehold at 240,000 dollars before listing it openly, with the balance to be met by a mortgage from the Commonage Bank agreed in principle at 60 percent of valuation. Shares are offered at 50 dollars, with a minimum holding of two shares and a maximum of 400, carrying one vote per member regardless of holding. Interest, targeted at 3 percent but payable solely at the board's discretion from surpluses, has been paid in two of the past four years. The bakery reports sales of 310,000 dollars last year, a surplus of 22,000 dollars, and eleven staff of whom seven are members. Risks stated include the departure of the head baker, whose sourdough process the prospectus calls, with unusual candor for such a document, the main asset not on the balance sheet; a succession plan places two apprentices under her instruction through next year. If the minimum is not reached by the closing date of March 15, subscriptions are returned in full. The offer document was reviewed under the community shares standard mark.
question: At what price is the freehold offered to the cooperative?

passage: Notice of enforcement action, Office of Petroleum Storage Compliance, facility 2071, the former Redpoll Service Station, Cobb Street. Inspection of April 8 found that the facility's three underground tanks, out of service since the station closed in 2019, have not been permanently closed within the 24 months the rule allows for temporary closure status. Tightness testing conducted at the owner's expense on April 22 found tanks 1 and 2 tight; tank 3, a 4,000 gallon gasoline tank, failed, and soil borings adjacent to it returned petroleum concentrations above the reporting threshold in two of five samples, at depths of eight and eleven feet. The owner, the estate of Emory Redpoll, is ordered to: remove all three tanks within 120 days; excavate impacted soil under the direction of a licensed environmental professional; and submit a site assessment report within 60 days of removal. The estate's application to the orphaned tank fund, which reimburses eligible costs above a 10,000 dollar deductible to a cap of 400,000 dollars, has been accepted for processing, the station having operated before the insurance requirement of 1989. A groundwater monitoring decision is deferred pending the site assessment. Penalties are held in abeyance conditioned on the schedule above.
question: Which tank failed the tightness testing?

passage: Annual report to the Charity Registry, the Lanthorn Night Shelter, registration 8814. The shelter operated 31 beds on all 365 nights, provided 10,700 bed nights at an occupancy of 95 percent, and turned away, for want of space, an average of four persons nightly in the January to March quarter, the figure the trustees ask the Registry to weigh in the pending application to extend into the adjoining ropewalk building. Income of 610,000 dollars comprised county contract payments of 380,000 dollars, donations of 170,000 dollars, and charity shop surplus of 60,000 dollars, the shop on Tanyard Street having traded for its first full year under volunteer management. Expenditure of 588,000 dollars included wages for a staff of 14, food, and utilities, the last item up 34 percent on the prior year. The trustees draw attention to a single restricted fund matter: a donation of 45,000 dollars received in November for conversion of the ropewalk, held unspent pending planning consent, and returnable under its terms if consent is refused by next December. Outcomes reported under the county contract: 96 residents moved to settled accommodation, against a target of 80, and 61 remained settled at six months. The auditor's opinion is unqualified. Trustee meetings numbered eleven with attendance averaging 84 percent.
question: How many residents moved to settled accommodation during the year?

passage: Petition for variance from the noise ordinance, filed by the Blackfriars Forge and Metal Arts School with the town clerk of Denholm, file N-2288. The school, teaching traditional smithing to classes of eight at the former wheelwright shop, seeks relief from the ordinance's daytime limit of 60 decibels at the property line, measured exceedances having ranged to 71 decibels during power hammer instruction. The petition proposes: limiting power hammer use to the hours of 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. on weekdays; installation of an acoustic enclosure around the 50 kilogram hammer, engineered per the enclosed specification to reduce line readings to 63 decibels; and cessation of all forging on the four summer Saturdays of the village fair. The school notes that hand forging, the bulk of instruction, measures below the limit, and that the shop operated as a working forge from 1840 until 1961 before the ordinance's adoption in 1978. Fourteen letters accompany the petition: nine in support, including the two nearest neighbors, who cite the school's repair of the shared boundary wall; five opposed, chiefly from the Croft Lane houses downwind. The acoustics consultant's fee schedule and the enclosure quotation of 23,000 dollars are annexed. The hearing is set before the select board on August 19.
question: To what level is the acoustic enclosure engineered to reduce property line readings?

passage: Certificate of need application, Dunwich Valley Health District, for a fixed magnetic resonance imaging unit at the Coleford community hospital. The district operates the valley's only hospital, of 48 beds, and refers imaging patients either to a mobile unit visiting Tuesdays or to the regional center at Asche, 62 road miles distant over the pass. The application documents 2,900 scans referred out in the latest year, of which 640 were completed on the mobile unit, constrained by its single day schedule, and the remainder at Asche, with a median wait of 23 days and a winter cancellation rate on the pass road of 9 percent. The proposed unit, costed at 2.4 million dollars installed, projects 2,200 scans in year one, rising to 2,800 by year three, against a break even of 1,900; staffing requires two technologists, one recruited, and teleradiology reading under the existing Asche contract. The regional review board's standard, requiring 2,000 projected scans within a 45 minute drive population, is met by the district's calculation of 2,450, which counts the three upland townships added to the district by the 2020 boundary revision. One competing comment, from the Asche center, disputes the drive time analysis. Decision is due within 120 days.
question: What is the break even number of annual scans for the proposed unit?
